q: 1. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a push of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under a compressive push, the bar shortens (length decreases) and expands laterally (width and thickness increase).

q: 2. The volumetric strain is the ratio of the
options: original thickness to the change in thickness
change in thickness to the original thickness
original volume to the change in volume
change in volume to the original volume
explain: Volumetric strain measures the overall deformation of a body in terms of volume change relative to its initial state.

q: 3. When a body is subjected to three mutually perpendicular stresses, of equal intensity, the ratio of direct stress to the corresponding volumetric strain is
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) is the ratio of direct stress to volumetric strain when a body is subjected to equal stresses in all three directions.

q: 4. The ratio of bulk modulus to Young's modulus for a Poisson's ratio of 0.25 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 3K(1 - 2μ). If μ = 0.25, then E = 3K(1 - 0.5) = 1.5K. Therefore, K/E = 1/1.5 = 2/3.

q: 5. The ratio of shear modulus to the modulus of elasticity for a Poisson's ratio of 0.4 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 2G(1 + μ). If μ = 0.4, then E = 2G(1.4) = 2.8G. Therefore, G/E = 1/2.8 = 5/14.

q: 6. The Young's modulus of a material is 125 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.25. The modulus of rigidity of the material is
7. Within elastic limit, shear stress is ___________ shear strain.
explain: According to Hooke's Law for shear, shear stress is directly proportional to shear strain within the elastic limit.

q: 8. Shear modulus is the ratio of
explain: Shear Modulus (or Modulus of Rigidity, G) is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

q: 9. A localized compressive stress at the area of contact between two members is known as
explain: Crushing stress (or bearing stress) is the localized compressive stress at the surface of contact between two relative parts.

q: 10. In a bar of large length when held vertically, its own weight produces additional stress. The maximum stress will be
options: at every point of the bar
explain: The top cross-section must support the weight of the entire bar below it, making the stress maximum at the support.

q: 11. If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section becomes
explain: This refers to the theoretical 'limit of length' for a bar under its own weight; if the self-weight stress equals the allowed stress, any increase in length would require an infinite area to maintain that stress level.

q: 12. The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length, is
explain: Elongation of prismatic bar = γL²/2E. Elongation of conical bar = γL²/6E. The ratio is (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3.

q: 13. If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the proportion of maximum stress will increase in the ratio
explain: Stress due to self-weight is σ = γL. If all dimensions increase by n, the new length is nL, so stress becomes n(γL), a ratio of n:1.

q: 14. If the stress in each cross-section of a pillar is equal to its working stress, it is called
explain: A body of equal strength is designed so that the stress is constant at all sections, usually by varying the cross-sectional area.

q: 15. A member with cross-section A mm² is subjected to a force P N. It is L mm long. The linear strain will be
explain: Stress σ = P/A. Strain ε = σ/E = P/(AE). Strain is dimensionless (mm/mm).

q: 16. Young's Modulus is the ratio of the normal stress to the
explain: By definition, Young's Modulus is the constant of proportionality between normal stress and normal strain within the limit of proportionality.

q: 17. As per elastic theory of design, the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: unlimited load to load at yield
explain: Factor of Safety (FOS) is defined as the ratio of the failure stress (yield stress for ductile materials) to the allowable or working stress.

q: 18. In a composite bar, the load distribution... is based on the assumption that all the materials will have
explain: For composite bars subjected to axial loads, the fundamental compatibility condition is that the change in length is the same for all components, meaning they undergo the same strain.

q: 19. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
options: supporting conditions at the two ends
explain: Thermal stress only develops if the expansion or contraction of the member is restricted by the supporting conditions (e.g., fixed ends).

q: 20. In a Uniaxial tension test on a mild steel bar, the Lueders' lines will be
options: inclined at 45° to the direction of tensile stress
perpendicular to the direction of tensile stress
along the direction of tensile stress
explain: Lueders' lines (or slip lines) appear due to shear failure, which occurs on planes of maximum shear stress, typically inclined at 45° to the axis of tensile loading.

q: 21. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation before rupture, measured by percentage elongation.

q: 22. The percentage reduction in area of a member from a direct tension test indicates
explain: Like elongation, the reduction in cross-sectional area at the point of fracture is a key measure of a material's ductility.

q: 23. The Poisson's ratio is the ratio of
options: Yong's Modulus elasticity to Modulus of Rigidity
explain: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of transverse (lateral) strain to axial (longitudinal) strain.

q: 24. A tie is a member which
options: is subjected to axial tension primarily
explain: In structural engineering, a 'tie' is a tension member designed to resist forces that pull it apart.

q: 25. The product of Young's modulus (E) and moment of inertia (I) is known as
explain: Flexural rigidity (EI) represents the resistance offered by a beam section against bending deformation.

q: 26. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress develops on
explain: In a standard sagging beam, the fibers above the neutral axis are in compression, with the maximum value occurring at the outermost 'top' fiber.

q: 27. The region of the cross-section of a column in which compressive load may be applied without producing any tensile stress, is known as the core... in circular columns the radius of the core, is
explain: To avoid tension in a circular section (Middle Fourth Rule), the eccentricity must not exceed D/8 from the center, making the radius of the core R/4 (or D/8).

q: 28. Stress in members of statically determinate simple frames, can be determined by
explain: All three are standard methods for analyzing trusses; Method of Joints uses joint equilibrium, Method of Sections uses part equilibrium, and Graphical (Cremona) uses vector diagrams.

q: 29. A principal plane is a plane which carries
options: the given of higher magnitude acting
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which the shear stress is zero; they only carry normal stresses (principal stresses).

q: 30. The angle between the two principal planes is
explain: The major and minor principal planes are always mutually perpendicular (90 degrees apart).

q: 31. If an element of a specimen of brittle material is subjected to shear stress, the crack propagation if occurs, will be inclined to the sides of the element at
explain: Brittle materials are weak in tension. Pure shear produces maximum principal tensile stress at 45°, leading to failure along that plane.

q: 32. A prismatic bar is supported at top and is subjected to its own weight... the total elongation of the bar is given by
explain: The elongation due to self-weight is WL/2AE. Substituting W = ρAL, we get (ρAL)L/2AE = ρl²/2E.

q: 33. The moment of inertia of triangular section b x d, about the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_base = I_cg + Ah² = (bh³/36) + (1/2 bh)(h/3)² = bh³/12.

q: 34. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum tensile stress is developed on the
explain: For a simply supported beam under downward loads, the beam sags. This creates compression in the top fibers and tension in the bottom fibers.

q: 35. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress is developed on the
explain: As explained in Q. 296, the curvature causes the top layer of a simply supported beam to shorten, resulting in maximum compressive stress.

q: 36. The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on the configuration
explain: While max shear is at the neutral axis for common shapes like rectangles/circles, for certain complex sections (like some I-beams), it can occur elsewhere depending on the geometry.

q: 37. The shear stress at any section of a shaft is maximum
options: at the centre of the section
at a distance r/2 from the centre
at the top of the surface
at a distance 3/4r from the centre
explain: In torsion, shear stress τ = (T·r)/J. It is zero at the center (axis of rotation) and increases linearly to a maximum at the outer surface (radius R).

q: 38. The ratio of maximum shear stress developed in a rectangular beam and a circular beam of the same cross-sectional area is
explain: Ratio = (1.5 for rectangle) / (1.33 for circle) = (3/2) / (4/3) = 9/8.

q: 39. A beam of triangular section is placed with its base horizontal. The maximum shear stress occurs at
options: centre of gravity of the triangle
explain: Unlike rectangular sections, the maximum shear stress in a triangular section occurs at h/2 (mid-height), whereas the neutral axis is at h/3 from the base.

q: 40. The ratio of maximum shear stress to average shear stress in the case of a rectangular section is
explain: As noted in Q. 301, the maximum shear stress for a rectangle is 1.5 times (3/2) the average shear stress.

q: 41. In the case of H section the maximum shear stress will occur at
options: at the junction of the web and flanges
explain: In an H-section (similar to an I-section), the maximum shear stress is located at the neutral axis of the cross-section.

q: 42. For the materials which do not have a pronounced yield point... the yield point is taken to be
options: stress corresponding to 0.2% strain from the stress strain curve
the stress at which the permanent set reaches the value 0.2%
average of ultimate strength and actual breaking stress
explain: For materials like aluminum or high-strength steel, the proof stress (yield point) is determined using the 0.2% offset method.

q: 43. In the case of uniaxial tension the angle between the plane carrying maximum shear stress and direction of tensile force will be
explain: Under uniaxial tension, maximum shear stress occurs on planes inclined at 45° to the axis of the load.

q: 44. An element is subjected to two normal stress σ1 and σ2... The max shear stress is given by
explain: The maximum in-plane shear stress is equal to half the difference between the principal stresses: τ_max = (σ1 - σ2)/2.

q: 45. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then normal stress on an oblique section... inclined at angle θ to the normal... is
explain: The normal stress on an oblique plane is σ_n = σ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the normal to the plane and the direction of stress.

q: 46. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then tangential or shear stress on an oblique section... inclined at angle θ to the normal... is
explain: The tangential (shear) stress on an oblique plane is given by τ = (σ/2) sin 2θ.

q: 47. The resultant stress on an inclined plane which is inclined at an angle θ to the normal cross-section... is
explain: The resultant stress on a plane inclined at θ is the vector sum of normal and tangential stress, which simplifies to σ cosθ for a single axial stress.

q: 48. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then maximum normal stress occurs at a section inclined at
explain: Normal stress is σ cos²θ. This is maximum when cos θ = 1, which occurs at θ = 0° (the plane perpendicular to the force).

q: 49. A body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane. The shear stress is maximum at a section inclined at ............ to the normal of the section.
explain: Shear stress is (σ/2) sin 2θ. This is maximum when sin 2θ = 1 (at 2θ = 90° or 270°), giving θ = 45° and 135°.

q: 50. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, the maximum shear stress is ............ the maximum normal stress.
explain: Maximum normal stress is σ (at 0°), and maximum shear stress is σ/2 (at 45°). Therefore, max shear is half of max normal stress.
